_meta.source: CL = Código Limpo (Robert C. Martin), pages of the scanned PDF
_meta.note: items are phrased as questions; each ref points to the rule in references/ and cc_index.json; area keys stay in Portuguese (nomes, funcoes, ...)

items.q: Does every name reveal its intent, without needing a comment?
Does no name misinform (e.g. 'List' for something that is not a list) or look almost identical to another?
Are the distinctions meaningful, with no number series (a1, a2) or noise words (Info, Data)?
Are the names pronounceable and searchable; does the length follow the scope?
Are there no encodings (Hungarian notation, m_ prefix, I on interfaces)?
Is there no mental mapping (single letters outside small loops)?
Are classes nouns and methods verbs?
Is there one word per concept and no puns (the same name with different meanings)?
Do the names use the solution or problem domain and have meaningful context, without gratuitous prefixes?
Are the functions small (at most 20 lines; the book's ideal is 2 to 4)?
Are if/else/while blocks one line long and is indentation at one or two levels?
Does each function do one thing (no other function can be extracted with a name that is not a restatement of the implementation)?
Are all the statements of the function at the same level of abstraction, and does the code read top to bottom (Stepdown Rule)?
Does any switch appear only once, hidden in a factory that creates polymorphic objects?
Is the number of arguments zero, one or two (triads avoided; more than three only for a very special reason)?
Is there no boolean argument (flag) that gives the function two behaviors?
Were too many arguments grouped into an object?
Does the function have no hidden side effects or output arguments?
Does the function do something or answer something, but not both (command-query separation)?
Are errors exceptions (not return codes) and was the try/catch body extracted into its own function?
Is there no duplication?
Is every comment necessary, or can it be replaced by a function or variable with a good name?
Do the remaining comments explain intent, clarify, or warn about consequences?
Are there no redundant, misleading or rule-mandated comments (Javadoc on everything)?
Is there no change journal, credits or authorship in the code (version control keeps that)?
Is there no commented-out code?
Are there no closing brace comments, position markers or noise?
Are the TODOs reviewed and do they not justify bad code?
Do the comments avoid nonlocal or excessive information, or an inobvious connection to the code?
Does the team follow a single set of formatting rules, preferably automated?
Does the file read like a newspaper (high level at the top) and are concepts separated by blank lines?
Are related concepts close together, local variables near their use, and the calling function above the called one?
Do instance variables sit in a well-known place (in Java, at the top of the class)?
Do the lines fit the limit the author uses (120 characters)?
Do spaces indicate relationship and precedence, without artificial horizontal alignment?
Is every scope indented, with no short if/while/function collapsed into one line?
Does the class expose abstractions of the data, rather than automatic getters/setters for every field?
Is it clear whether each type is an object (hides data, exposes functions) or a data structure (exposes data)?
Are there no hybrids, half object and half data structure?
Does the code respect the Law of Demeter (no train wrecks navigating the insides of objects)?
Do DTOs and Active Records contain no business rules?
Does it use exceptions instead of return codes, without obscuring the logic?
Did the code that may throw an exception start with try-catch-finally and with tests that force the exception?
Does it use unchecked exceptions (except in a critical library)?
Do exceptions carry context (operation and type of failure) and are they defined by the needs of whoever catches them?
Are third-party APIs wrapped, converting their exceptions?
Do business cases use Special Case instead of an exception?
Does the code not return null (throw an exception, return a Special Case or an empty list)?
Does the code not pass null as an argument?
Are boundary interfaces (e.g. Map) encapsulated and kept from circulating through the public API?
Are there learning/boundary tests that exercise the third-party API the way your code uses it?
For an API that does not exist yet, is there an interface of your own connected by an ADAPTER?
Is external code referenced in few places?
Was the production code written after a failing test (three laws of TDD)?
Is the test code as clean as the production code?
Is each test readable and does it follow BUILD-OPERATE-CHECK (CONSTRUIR-OPERAR-VERIFICAR), with no details that do not serve its intent?
Is there a test API/DSL that hides repetitive details?
Does each test check a single concept, with few assertions?
Are the tests F.I.R.S.T.: fast, independent, repeatable, self-validating and timely?
Does the class follow the order: public constants, private statics, instance variables, public functions, and private ones right after their caller?
Is the class small in responsibilities and can it be described in ~25 words without 'if', 'and', 'or', 'but'?
Does the class have one, and only one, reason to change (SRP)?
Is cohesion high (few instance variables, used by most methods)?
Do new features enter by extension, without changing existing classes (OCP)?
Does the client depend on abstractions, received through the constructor (DIP)?
Is object construction separated from use (main, factories or dependency injection)?
Are cross-cutting concerns (persistence, transactions, security) not scattered through the business logic?
Is the domain logic in testable POJOs, and were decisions postponed until the last responsible moment?
Do standards and frameworks come in only when they add demonstrable value?

design-simples.title: Emergence (the four rules of simple design)

items.q: Do all the tests run and pass?
Is there no duplication (not even of implementation)?
Does the code express intent (names, small functions and classes, named patterns, tests as documentation)?
Is the number of classes and methods the minimum, without dogmas such as one interface per class?
Is the concurrent code separated from the rest (SRP)?
Is access to shared data minimal, with copies and independent threads when possible?
Does it use the concurrency library (thread-safe collections, Executor, atomic classes) instead of manual threads?
Is there no dependency between synchronized methods called in sequence by the client?
Are the synchronized sections as small as possible?
Was shutdown thought through from the start?
Is at least one of the four deadlock conditions broken (e.g. global acquisition order)?
Do the tests run with more threads than processors, on several platforms, with instrumentation to force failures?
